clue.text: Greeting to bishop (in a small way) that isn't one for total immersion

definitions.text: that isn't one for total immersion

parts.note: hi is an informal greeting

indicators.note: the bishop is placed in the small way, its letter going inside the word for a path

parts.note: a path is a small way or track
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A churchman is greeted modestly, though not in a way that involves full baptism by immersion.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis reads as a modest aside, but 'in' there is the container signal, putting the bishop inside the small way.
explanation.definitionFit: A hip bath is a small tub you sit in with legs outside, so the body is never fully submerged.

clue.text: Hearts are associated with March

parts.note: H is the card-suit abbreviation for hearts
taken as written

explanation.surface: Love is linked to the month of March, perhaps a spring romance.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'March hare' of proverb and Alice in Wonderland is the animal tied to March; the answer is also David Hare, the playwright, one of the theme's dramatists.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'mad as a March hare' links the animal firmly to March, its breeding season.

clue.text: Arrange for your head to be contending with Ruth

parts.note: to pit someone is to arrange for them to be set against another, which the clue spells out as 'to be contending'

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only the start of 'your' is used

explanation.surface: Someone schemes to have your leader fight a woman called Ruth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arrange for ... to be contending' together describes PIT (set against); the words 'to be contending' finish that phrase around 'your head', Y. Ruth is the old word for compassion, as in 'ruthless'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruth is an archaic noun for compassion or sorrow for another, surviving in ruthless; it is a synonym.

clue.text: I caused a stir with "A Fool on a Hill"

parts.note: a git is a British insult for a stupid person
taken as written
a tor is a rocky hill, especially on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A painting or song called 'A Fool on a Hill' proudly claims to have made a fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' places the fool above the hill: A, GIT, A, TOR in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabble-rouser stirs up trouble, so one speaking as 'I caused a stir' describes that kind of person.

clue.text: Violent character not easy to read

definitions.meaning: a hired thug or tough guy, as in a gangster film
dense and laborious, as in hard-going prose

explanation.surface: A thug in a novel that is hard going.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy is a hired tough in slang, and heavy reading is dense or laborious.

clue.text: The relative proposition

parts.note: taken as written
sis, short for sister, is a relative

explanation.surface: A family member puts forward an idea.
explanation.definitionFit: A thesis is a proposition put forward to be argued or proved, a direct synonym.

clue.text: 1 down's right about former drink coming to him

indicators.note: the first pieces surround the next ones, as 'about' places them around

parts.note: the answer to 1 down is the playwright's surname, the hare; the 's means 'has'
old means former, as in an old flame
a pint is a drink of beer

explanation.surface: The playwright from 1 down has the right to a pint of the old stuff coming his way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'him' is one of the theme's playwrights listed at 14 down. 'about' has the HARER outer pair split after its third letter to take in the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun points at one of the dramatists that 14 down gathers together, this one a Nobel-winning playwright.

clue.text: That's right about climber with a break he spends on addiction

indicators.note: the Latin word surrounds the other pieces, as 'about' places it around them

parts.note: sic, Latin for 'thus', marks a quotation as right as written
the hop is a climbing plant
taken as written
hol is short for holiday, a break

explanation.surface: Someone confirms that a mountaineer on a break spends compulsively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climber' suggests a mountaineer, but it is the hop plant that climbs poles.
explanation.definitionFit: A compulsive shopper is a person who spends money as an addiction, the sense this phrase describes.

clue.text: Byway, small, that is OK, say Geordies

parts.note: id est is the Latin for 'that is', shortened to i.e.
reet is northern English dialect for right or all right; Geordies are people from Tyneside

explanation.surface: A small lane is described as fine by people from Newcastle.
explanation.walkthrough: Geordies are natives of Newcastle upon Tyne in north-east England, where 'reet' means right or all right.
explanation.definitionFit: A side street is a minor road off a main one, and byway means a minor road or lane.

clue.text: See 29
He ran off with ex-king entering German river

indicators.note: something gone off is spoiled, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: ex means former, which is old

indicators.note: the king goes into the river's name, as entering means going inside

parts.note: the Weser is a river in north-west Germany
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A man eloped with a deposed monarch who was crossing a river in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' makes ARN from RAN; then OLD, then K entering WESER gives WESKER. 'He' is one of the theme's dramatists listed at 14 down.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun stands for one of the playwrights 14 down gathers, here the author of Roots and Chips with Everything.

clue.text: See 6
Shirley's boy with root vegetables: am I going to interrupt?

parts.note: a lad is a boy

indicators.note: the question breaks into the vegetables' name, as interrupting means coming between

parts.note: yams are starchy tuber vegetables
'will I' asks the same as 'am I going to'

explanation.surface: Shirley's son eats yams and asks whether he may butt in.
explanation.walkthrough: Shirley Williams, a British politician, became Baroness Williams, so 'Shirley' is defined by her title; the question breaks the vegetables after their first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Shirley Williams, founder of the SDP, became a life peer, so she is formally styled by this title.

clue.text: Ephemeral revolts hid problem

indicators.note: a problem means things are in disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An uprising that briefly concealed a difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ephemeral lasts a very short time, the same meaning as a brief life.

clue.text: 1 down, 9, 11, 16, 21 and 29, having a drink, ordered 'Sit!', sat

parts.note: a dram is a small drink, usually of whisky

indicators.note: set in order means rearranged, so these letters are reshuffled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A group of playwrights at the bar were told to sit, and obeyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' looks like the command was given, but it is the anagram signal for the two short words that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: The listed answers are all playwrights: Hare, Rattigan, Pinter, Wesker, Plater and Terence.

clue.text: University man to disturb the peace with some power

parts.note: he is the pronoun for a man
to riot is to disturb the peace
a watt is a unit of power

explanation.surface: A student causes trouble with a show of strength.
explanation.walkthrough: HERIOT-WATT is a university in Edinburgh, Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Heriot-Watt is a Scottish university in Edinburgh, named after George Heriot and James Watt.

clue.text: See 10
See 19
Canonised forester's new baby?

parts.note: a canonised person is a saint, abbreviated St
a ranger looks after a forest

explanation.surface: A sainted woodsman becomes a father.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as playful: a newborn is someone nobody has met before.
explanation.definitionFit: A newborn baby is, whimsically, someone new to everyone, an unknown person arriving in the family.

clue.text: Talk of the spirit of the Guardian

parts.note: rum is a spirit
this puzzle is in the Guardian, so 'of the Guardian' is 'our' from the paper's view

explanation.surface: Gossip about the newspaper's drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: The Guardian speaks of itself as 'we', so what belongs to it is 'our'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rumour is talk or hearsay passed around, so talk is a fair synonym here.

clue.text: English father accepts French call to desk

indicators.note: the father takes in the next pieces, as accepting means receiving inside

parts.note: a sire is a father
cri is French for a cry or call
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Englishman's father agrees to a summons from France to report to his desk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accepts' means the father's name opens after its first letter to take in the French call and 'to'.
explanation.definitionFit: An escritoire is a small writing desk with drawers and compartments.

clue.text: See 24
Lilliputian, one of ten eliminated one by one if I replace energy

indicators.note: one letter stands in place of another, signalled by replace

parts.words: one of ten eliminated one by one
parts.note: the counting rhyme 'Ten Little Indians' sees them eliminated one at a time, so one of them is a little Indian
taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A tiny person, one of ten picked off in turn, is swapped for some vigour.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gulliver's Travels, Lilliput's Little-Endians open eggs at the small end. The clue's order is loose: E takes I's place in the rhyme's figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Little-Endians are a faction of Lilliput in Swift's satire, so a member is a Lilliputian.

clue.text: Both sides of door have 12 inches leeway

indicators.note: both sides of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: 12 inches is one foot, 1 FT, with 1 written as I

explanation.surface: A door has an inch of clearance each side.
explanation.walkthrough: '12 inches' is 1 FT, the figure 1 read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Drift is a margin of deviation, as leeway is the sideways drift of a ship.

clue.text: He will make a plan in due course

indicators.note: to make a plan is to construct it, so these letters are rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written
later means in due course

explanation.surface: Someone promises to draw up a scheme eventually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make' rearranges A PLAN into ALANP. 'He' is one of the playwrights listed at 14 down.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun stands for one of the dramatists gathered by 14 down, here a writer of television drama.

clue.text: Such and 2 was said of Hamlet's madness, giving time to repent

definitions.text: Such and 2 was said of Hamlet's madness

parts.note: to rue is to regret or repent

explanation.surface: Polonius's verdict on the prince's madness gives one time for repentance.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet, Polonius says of Hamlet's madness: "'tis true 'tis pity, and pity 'tis 'tis true" — 2 down supplies the other word.
explanation.definitionFit: Polonius's line pairs the two words, so the quotation itself defines the one not given by 2 down.

clue.text: Little girl is in Parliament and pays calls

parts.note: Vi is short for Violet or Victoria
an MP sits in Parliament

explanation.surface: A young girl is an MP and settles debts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pays calls' looks like settling bills; it means drops in on people.
explanation.definitionFit: To pay calls on people is to drop in on them socially, the same as dropping by their homes.

clue.text: The odd one?

parts.note: odd can mean strange, and one is a grammatical number, so the word means both peculiar and not plural

explanation.surface: Picking out the misfit in a group.
explanation.definitionFit: Singular means remarkable or strange, and in grammar it denotes a single one rather than many.

clue.text: Rat in the sand

definitions.meaning: to rat is to abandon or betray, to leave one's side
a barren sandy region like the Sahara

explanation.surface: A rodent burrowing in the dunes.
explanation.definitionFit: To desert is to rat on someone, and a desert is a sandy waste.

clue.text: Cigarette? Tanner would get it for him

indicators.note: the letters are reworked to get him, as getting it for someone means making it out of materials

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tanning salon worker would buy a smoke for a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: CIGARETTE and TANNER give the fifteen letters. 'him' is one of the playwrights listed at 14 down.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun names one of the dramatists 14 down gathers, author of The Winslow Boy.
